newsitem.title: USA: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.
newsitem.headline: Fed expected to hold interest rates steady.

text.p: By Rich Miller, Economics Correspondent
Federal Reserve policy-makers are expected to decide this week to hold interest rates steady amid signs that the economy has cooled off as the weather has heated up, economists and analysts said.
"Fireworks at the Fed appear remote," said Joel Naroff, chief economist at Philadelphia-based First Union Corp.
Inflation is low and stable. Economic growth is slowing from the first quarter's rambunctious rate, and Wall Street is not calling for another central bank rate increase.

A survey of 18 top economists by St. Louis-based Macroeconomic Advisers found that all but three expect the central bank's policy-making Federal Open Market Committee to leave rates unchanged at its meeting on Tuesday and Wednesday.

In an effort to prevent the economy from overheating and to extend the expansion, the central bank tightened credit in March for the first time in more than two years, bumping up a key short-term rate by a quarter percentage point, to 5.5 percent.

Since then, the economy has slowed sharply, to an annualized pace of between 1.5 percent and 2.0 percent in the second quarter, from a sizzling 5.9 percent rate in the first, the fastest clip in more than nine years.
"The slowdown has come quicker and more abruptly than many people had expected," said Joel Prakken, Chairman of Macroeconomic Advisers. "It has kind of frozen everybody."

Politics also would seem to argue against a rate rise now, analysts said. Central bank Chairman Alan Greenspan is slated to present the Fed's semi-annual assessment of the economy to Congress on July 22 and he would find it hard to defend a rate hike to lawmakers when growth is slowing and inflation low.

"I wouldn't want to be Alan Greenspan up in front of Congress explaining why he's just tightened," said David Wyss, senior economist at Massachusetts-based consultants DRI/McGraw Hill. "And I think he feels the same away."

The Fed's March 25 rate rise drew what Greenspan himself has acknowledged was more than the normal amount of criticism. Some analysts believe those attacks may have helped convince the Fed to hold rates steady at its last meeting, on May 20.
Fed officials admitted that it would not be easy to justify another rate increase now, but they said that would not stop the central bank from acting if it saw a need to do so.
Some economists, including those at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank, believe that it is only a matter of time before the Fed tightens credit further.
"They need an excuse to tighten," was how James Griffin, investment strategist at Connecticutt-based Aeltus Investment Management, put it.
They could find it before too long.

The economy's second-quarter lull is widely expected to prove temporary. With unemployment at a 23-year low, consumer confidence at a 27-year high and the stock market at record levels, all the ingredients for a rebound are in place.
"The underlying fundamentals are good," Macroeconomic Advisers' Prakken said. "It's sensible to expect a rebound in the third quarter. The question is how strong of one."

With the economy already running at or above capacity, it would not take much of a rebound to raise the risk of faster inflation, analysts said. The unemployment rate is already at levels that in the past led to stepped-up wage demands and eventually higher inflation.
At their two-day meeting this week, Fed policy-makers are also expected to update their economic forecast for this year and discuss projections for next year.

In February, they forecast growth this year of between 2 percent and 2.25 percent and consumer price inflation of between 2.75 percent and 3 percent. Analysts expect the former to be revised upward to take account of the strong growth of the first quarter. The latter is likely to be little changed.
